title: What Permits Do I Need for My Construction Project in Westchester NY
excerpt: Every Westchester municipality requires permits for construction work, but the process varies by town. Here's what you need to know before starting your project.
content:
If you're planning a renovation, addition, or new build in Westchester County, you're going to need permits. There's no way around it, and you shouldn't try. The permit process exists to keep homes safe and protect property values across the county.

The challenge is that every town handles permits differently. Scarsdale has its own building department. So does Rye, Bronxville, Larchmont, Mamaroneck, and Pelham. Each municipality sets its own rules, fees, and timelines. This isn't unique to one town or another. It's just how Westchester works.

What Types of Permits You'll Actually Need

The permits required depend on what you're building or changing. A kitchen remodel in Westchester usually needs a building permit because you're touching plumbing, electrical, and sometimes structural elements. A bathroom renovation typically requires the same. A second-story addition or primary suite addition will definitely need permits, along with site plan approval from your town.

Historic restorations in towns like Tarrytown, Hastings-on-Hudson, and Dobbs Ferry often require extra approval from local historic commissions. Open-concept conversions that remove walls need a licensed architect in Westchester, NY to sign off on structural changes. Custom new construction requires the most permits of all because you're building from the ground up.

The basic rule: if it changes the structure, plumbing, electrical, or mechanical systems of your home, you need a permit. If it's cosmetic only (paint, trim, fixtures), you probably don't.

Why Having a Licensed Architect and Contractor Matters

This is where working with a design-build firm in Westchester actually saves you time and headaches. When your architect and general contractor are the same person or team, there's no finger-pointing about who handles what. Silvio M. Luca is both a licensed architect in New York and a licensed general contractor. He manages every project personally, which means the drawings submitted to your building department are the same ones used during construction.

If you hire separate architects and contractors, they each have their own workflow. The architect submits plans. The contractor builds. If there's a problem, they blame each other. With a design-build approach, that doesn't happen.

The Town-by-Town Permit Process

Here's what to expect. You submit drawings and an application to your town's building department. In Harrison, Eastchester, or Ardsley, the review takes a few weeks typically. In White Plains or New Rochelle, it might take longer because those departments handle higher volume. The building official will either approve, request revisions, or deny. If they request changes, you resubmit and wait again.

Some towns require a zoning variance if your addition or new construction doesn't meet setback or height requirements. Towns like Pelham Manor and Tuckahoe are thorough about this. Others are stricter on environmental reviews if your lot is near wetlands.

Once the building permit is issued, you're cleared to start construction. But you'll need inspections along the way. Framing inspections, electrical inspections, plumbing inspections, and a final inspection before you can occupy the space.

What You Should Do Right Now

Don't start any construction work before permits are approved. Don't assume one town's requirements are the same as the next. And don't try to figure out the process alone if you're not sure what you need.
